claims.claim: The Soil Conservation Service was established as a USDA agency in 1935 under the Soil Conservation and Domestic Allotment Act.
claims.episode_span: the federal government, through the Soil Conservation Service established in 1935, sought living ground covers that could hold soil on slopes
claims.supporting_quote: The service was transferred to the Department of Agriculture on March 23, 1935, and was shortly thereafter combined with other USDA units to form the Soil Conservation Service by the Soil Conservation and Domestic Allotment Act of 1935.

claims.claim: Government erosion-control programs distributed roughly 85 million kudzu seedlings, with payments to farmers who planted them.
claims.episode_span: Between 1935 and 1945 the Soil Conservation Service distributed roughly 85 million kudzu seedlings and rooted crowns
claims.source_title: Kudzu in the United States - Wikipedia
claims.supporting_quote: recommended the use of kudzu to help control erosion of slopes which led to the government-aided distribution of 85 million seedlings

claims.claim: Channing Cope, an Atlanta Constitution columnist and radio host, founded the Kudzu Club of America, which claimed a membership of about 20,000 in the early 1940s.
claims.episode_span: Channing Cope, a Georgia newspaperman and founder of the Kudzu Club of America, organized county chapters that promoted the vine as “the miracle plant” and claimed more than 20,000 members by 1943
claims.source_title: The True Story of Kudzu, the Vine That Never Truly Ate the South - Smithsonian Magazine
claims.supporting_quote: By the early 1940s, Cope had started the Kudzu Club of America, with a membership of 20,000 and a goal of planting eight million acres across the South.

claims.claim: U.S. Forest Service sampling finds kudzu occupies only about 227,000 acres of forestland to some degree, far less than the popular vine-that-ate-the-South image implies.
claims.episode_span: perhaps 227,000 acres of heavy infestation across the region—though lighter scattered populations are more widespread
claims.source_title: The True Story of Kudzu, the Vine That Never Truly Ate the South - Smithsonian Magazine
claims.supporting_quote: the U.S. Forest Service reports that kudzu occupies, to some degree, about 227,000 acres of forestland, an area about the size of a small county and about one-sixth the size of Atlanta

claims.claim: The USDA listed kudzu as a weed in 1970, and in 1997 the vine was placed on the Federal Noxious Weed List.
claims.episode_span: The Department of Agriculture listed kudzu as a common weed in 1970 and as a noxious weed in 1997, ending federal promotion
claims.source_title: Kudzu in the United States - Wikipedia
claims.supporting_quote: removed kudzu from a list of suggested cover plants and listed it as a weed in 1970. By 1997, the vine was placed on the "Federal Noxious Weed List."

claims.claim: Kudzu can grow up to a foot (0.3 m) of new vine per day.
claims.episode_span: its capacity to produce up to a foot of new growth per day during the growing season
claims.source_title: Kudzu in the United States - Wikipedia
claims.supporting_quote: The vine has a growth rate of 0.3 m (1 foot) every day. The maximum length the vine can reach is 30 m

claims.claim: In 1935, amid Dust Bowl-era dust storms, Congress declared war on soil erosion and the federal government enlisted kudzu as a primary erosion-control tool.
claims.episode_span: The Dust Bowl years had exposed the South’s long-standing erosion problem in dramatic fashion
claims.source_title: The True Story of Kudzu, the Vine That Never Truly Ate the South - Smithsonian Magazine
claims.supporting_quote: in 1935, as dust storms damaged the prairies, Congress declared war on soil erosion and enlisted kudzu as a primary weapon
